title: Abdur Rasheed vs Shahid on 10 December, 2025

Date of pronouncement 10.12.2025 Page no.1/19 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:13 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid JUDGMENT 1. By way of the present judgment, this Court proceeds to adjudicate upon and finally dispose of the complaint instituted by Sh. Abdur Rasheed (hereinafter referred to as "the complainant") against Sh. Shahid (hereinafter referred to as "the accused"), alleging commission of the offence punishable under Section 138 read with Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter, "the NI Act "). The proceedings emanate from the alleged dishonour of cheque bearing no. 086855 dated 10.03.2018, drawn by the accused on his bank account maintained with Corporation Bank, for a sum of ₹1,00,000/-. It is the case of the complainant that the said cheque was issued by the accused in his favour towards part discharge of a legally enforceable liability arising out of the regular credit purchase of fruits from the complainant. 2. It has been categorically averred by the complainant that he is the proprietor of a shop engaged in the business of fruits and vegetables and that he had regular commercial dealings with the accused on a credit basis. The complainant has stated that, during the period from March 2017 to April 2018, the accused purchased goods from him on credit on several occasions, in respect whereof the complainant raised multiple invoices reflecting the supply of fruits and vegetables to the accused. 3. That in discharge of part liability, the accused issued cheque bearing no. 086855 dated 10.03.2028 of Rs. 1,00,000/- (cheque in question) drawn on Corporation Bank, Sikandarabad Branch, U.P. That the accused requested the complainant to present the cheque on second week of May 2018 by assuring him that the same would be duly honoured upon presentation. 4. The complainant has further averred that the accused had accumulated an outstanding liability of ₹5,00,000/- towards the complainant on account of the aforesaid credit purchases. In discharge of the said liability, the accused issued three cheques in favour of the complainant. However, upon presentation, all the said Page no.2/19 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:16 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid cheques were returned unpaid by the banker of the accused. Despite the dishonour of the said cheques, the outstanding amount remained unpaid, resulting in the continuance of the accused's liability towards the complainant. 5. To the complainant's utter shock and dismay, upon presentation of the aforesaid cheque (hereinafter referred to as "the cheque in question") for encashment through his banker, Punjab National Bank, Okhla Industrial Area, Delhi, the same was returned unpaid vide return memo dated 23.05.2018 bearing the remarks "Funds Insufficient". The dishonour of the cheque, despite the prior assurances extended by the accused regarding its honour, constituted the immediate cause of action and set in motion the present proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 6. Upon being apprised of the dishonour of the cheque, the complainant promptly contacted the accused, who initially resorted to evasive explanations and assurances of imminent payment. However, despite repeated requests and opportunities, the accused ultimately failed to honour his commitment and failed to discharge the liability arising from the cheque. 7. Subsequent to the dishonour of the cheque, and in adherence to the statutory requirements enshrined under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the complainant, through its engaged counsel, caused to be issued a legal demand notice dated 29.05.2018, which was dispatched to the accused via registered post and courier. Through the said notice, the accused was unequivocally called upon to pay the dishonoured cheque amount within the prescribed statutory period of fifteen days from the date of receipt. The legal notice was addressed to the residential address of the accused, as furnished by him and reiterated in the body of the complaint. 8. As per the postal records placed on record, the notice was duly dispatched to the accused on 02.06.2018. However, despite the dispatch of the legal notice and the Digitally signed Page no.3/19 SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:18 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid lapse of the mandatory statutory period, the accused neither made the payment of the cheque amount nor issued any written reply or response controverting the liability. The deliberate failure of the accused to comply with the legal demand notice, even after the dishonour of the cheque, prompted the complainant to invoke the penal provisions of the NI Act . Accordingly, the complainant instituted the present complaint under Sections 138 and 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, seeking penal consequences against the accused for wilful default and for the enforcement of the statutory presumption of liability arising from the dishonoured negotiable instrument. 9. The complainant has categorically asserted that the conduct of the accused, in issuing a cheque that was returned unpaid on the ground of "Funds Insufficient," squarely attracts the penal provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It is further alleged that the act of the accused reflects a deliberate failure to honour his financial commitment despite due notice, thereby constituting a clear breach of the statutory mandate envisaged under the Act. 10. This deliberate act of default, when viewed in conjunction with the dishonour of the cheque on the ground of insufficiency of funds, made the complainant believe that the accused never possessed a bona fide intention to honour his financial commitments. The complainant has asserted that the sequence of events -- from the issuance of the cheque to its eventual dishonour -- unmistakably reveals a conscious and wilful breach of a legally enforceable obligation by the accused. Such conduct, as per the complainant, is not a mere instance of inadvertence or financial mismanagement but a deliberate evasion of liability, thereby squarely attracting the penal provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 11. Upon a careful perusal of the material placed on record along with the complaint, and after due examination of the complainant by way of pre-summoning evidence in accordance with the mandate of Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Digitally signed Page no.4/19 by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:20 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid this Court was satisfied that a prima facie case was made out against the accused for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The evidence adduced at the pre-summoning stage sufficiently disclosed the existence of a legally enforceable liability and the issuance of the cheque in question by the accused towards its discharge, followed by its dishonour due to insufficiency of funds. Accordingly, vide order dated 09.10.2018, this Court was pleased to take cognizance of the offence and summoned the accused to face trial for the alleged dishonour of cheque issued in discharge of a debt or liability, as contemplated under the statutory scheme of the NI Act . 12. The accused appeared on 06.02.2019 with his counsel, and was granted bail by this Court on the very same date. Pursuant to the grant of bail, the accused was directed to furnish requisite bail bonds, and accordingly, he had furnished his bail bonds which were accepted. Subsequently, upon satisfaction that a prima facie case existed warranting trial, this Court proceeded to frame notice under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ( CrPC ), which was duly served upon the accused on 18.09.2019. Upon being apprised of the substance of accusation, including the specific allegations pertaining to issuance and dishonour of the cheque in question, the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial, thereby necessitating the recording of evidence in the matter in accordance with law. The accused admitted his signatures on the cheque in question. 13. The accused has taken a defence denying the existence of any legally enforceable debt or liability towards the complainant. It is the specific case of the accused that the cheque in question was handed over after writing the date as 10.02.2018, with the understanding that the payment would be made through electronic transfer. The accused asserts that, at the request of the complainant, he made a NEFT transfer of ₹1,00,000/- on 13.02.2018, i.e., the exact amount of the cheque, and that the Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.10 Page no.5/19 16:46:23 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid complainant thereafter misused the cheque by altering the date to 10.03.2018, which alteration is stated to be apparent on the face of the cheque. 14. Thereafter, in support of its case, the complainant adopted his post-summoning evidence and tendered his evidence affidavit. Further more, the complainant examined himself and one Bank Witness Namely Ms Neelam Rajdhan, Manager, Punjab National Bank as CW-1 and CW-2 respectively. CW1 entered the witness box and relied upon the following documents in support of his case:- Sr. No. Exhibits Particulars 1. Ex.CW-1/A Evidence by way of Affidavit 2. Ex.CW-1/1 Original cheque bearing no. 086855 dated 10.03.2018 for Rs. 1,00,000/-. 3. Ex.CW-1/2 Cheque returning memo dt. 23.05.2018 with remarks 'funds insufficient'. 4. Ex.CW-1/3 Legal demand notice dated 29.05.2018. 5. Ex.CW-1/4 & Postal receipts Ex.CW1/5 6. Ex.CW-1/6 & Tracking reports Ex.CW-1/7 7. Ex.CW-1/8 & Courier receipts Ex.CW-1/9 8. Ex.CW-1/10 & Tracking reports of couriers. Ex.CW-1/11 15. The same was followed by extensive examination, cross-examination of CW-1 conducted on behalf of the accused and on 29.02.2024, CW-1 was discharged. CW-2, summoned bank witness was examined on 09.10.2019 at the pre summoning stage during which she has brought the details of the cheque no. 086855. Deposit and receiving of the cheque as Ex.CW-2/1 and Ex.CW-2/2, certificate of evidence as Ex.CW-2/3. She deposed thar the reason of dishonour of cheque for the reason 'funds insufficient'. 17. Upon completion of the complainant evidence, same was closed on 29.02.2024. 18. As the complainant did not wish to examine any other witness, hence the matter fixed for recording of statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and subsequent to the conclusion of the complainant's evidence, and in compliance with the procedural mandate under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the statement of the accused was recorded by the Court on 06.05.2024, thereby affording him an opportunity to personally explain the incriminating circumstances appearing against him in the prosecution evidence. The accused reiterated his defence as taken in his earlier statement recorded under section 251 CrPC. Accused chose to lead DE however, subsequently vide statement recorded on 29.07.2024, he stated that he didn't want to lead DE 19. Thereafter, the accused was given a chance to lead his defense, but he refused the same for which the present case was proceeded with final arguments. Final Arguments 20. Thereafter, this Court heard the final arguments advanced from both sides on 30.08.2025. 21. Learned counsel for the complainant has submitted that the case at hand straightforwardly establishes that the accused, in a clear act of dishonesty and with dishonest intention, issued the cheque in question in discharge of a legally enforceable liability. Despite the execution of the cheque and the assurance given by the accused that it would be honored upon presentation, the cheque was Digitally signed by Page no.7/19 SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:32 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid dishonoured due to "Funds Insufficient," as evidenced by the return memo on record. The accused, during the proceedings, did not deny his signature on the cheque. Instead, he sought to falsely assert that the cheque was given on 10.02.2018 and that he had made the payment on 13.02.2018, which is belied by the record and the unchallenged facts. 22. It was further argued that the legal requisites under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act have been fully satisfied: issuance of the cheque, the return of the cheque unpaid, within the statutory period, and non-payment after receipt of the legal demand notice. The accused's attempt to defend by claiming that the liability was settled is baseless, unsupported by evidence, and clearly a deliberate attempt to evade repayment. 23. It was further submitted that the accused's conduct amounts to cheating, as he issued the cheque with full knowledge of insufficient funds, with the ulterior motive to mislead and defraud the complainant. The conduct is condemnable, and the legal consequences mandated under the NI Act are clear and unambiguous. 24. Learned counsel also contends that the cheque was dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds and not being stale. It has been further averred that the alteration of the date does not have any bearing on thr case of the complainant. 25. Learned counsel has argued that the accused has failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. It is submitted that the defence raised by the accused--namely that the cheque was a blank security cheque and that repayments had been made--are not supported by any cogent evidence. It is emphasized that the issuance of a cheque, even by way of security, does not absolve the accused if the cheque is presented against an existing liability, as held by way of catena of judgments. Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 Page no.8/19 16:46:34 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid 26. Per contra, the learned counsel for the accused has contended that the cheque in question suffers from a material alteration with respect to the date, which goes to the root of the complainant's case. It is argued that when the cheque was handed over by the accused, it originally bore the date 10.02.2018 and not 10.03.2018, as presently reflected on the cheque. The said alteration, according to the defence, is clearly apparent on a bare perusal of the cheque itself and has not been explained by the complainant in accordance with law. 27. It is further submitted that subsequent to the issuance of the cheque dated 10.02.2018, the accused had already transferred an amount of ₹1,00,000/-, i.e., the exact cheque amount, to the complainant on 13.02.2018, which fact stands corroborated from the bank statement of the accused placed on record. In view of the said payment, it is contended that no legally enforceable debt or liability subsisted against the accused on the date of presentation of the cheque. 28. On the basis of the aforesaid submissions, the defence has argued that the cheque having been materially altered and the liability having already been discharged, the essential ingredients of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are not fulfilled, and therefore, the accused cannot be held liable under the said provision. Legal Analysis & Findings:- 29. I have heard at considerable length the detailed arguments advanced by the learned counsel appearing for the complainant as well as the learned counsel representing the accused. Their respective submissions have been carefully analysed in the context of the factual matrix and the legal principles applicable to the case. This Court has also undertaken a thorough and meticulous scrutiny of the entire judicial record, which includes the contents of the complaint, the affidavits and supporting documents annexed thereto, the oral testimonies of the complainant's and the defence witnesses recorded during the course of trial, and all exhibits relied upon by the respective parties. Each piece of evidence has been examined individually as Digitally signed Page no.9/19 SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:36 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid well as in conjunction with the other evidence on record so as to assess its evidentiary value, credibility, and probative strength. The rival submissions have been objectively evaluated against the backdrop of the statutory framework and the well-settled legal position governing proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Court has, therefore, endeavoured to reach a reasoned and just determination by adopting a holistic and balanced appreciation of the evidence and circumstances presented before it. 30. Before embarking upon a discussion on the merits of the present case, it is considered apposite to first delineate the legal framework governing the offence of dishonour of cheque, as encapsulated under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The legislative intent behind enacting Section 138 is to instill greater financial discipline and sanctity in contractual obligations by deterring the issuance of cheques without sufficient funds or without adequate arrangements with the banker. The provision prescribes penal consequences in the event of dishonor of a cheque on grounds of insufficiency of funds or if the amount exceeds the arrangement with the bank, thereby recognizing the cheque as a legitimate instrument of payment in the eyes of the law. 31. In order to fasten criminal liability upon an accused under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, it is incumbent upon the complainant to plead and prove the existence of certain foundational ingredients through the averments made in the complaint and the evidence led during the course of trial. The essential ingredients that must be cumulatively satisfied are as follows: a. That the accused must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him with a banker, for the payment of a certain sum of money to another person, and such payment must have been intended for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability; Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 Page no.10/19 16:46:38 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid b. That the said cheque must have been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it was drawn, or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; c. That upon such presentation, the cheque must have been returned unpaid by the bank, either due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's account or because the amount exceeded the arrangement made by the drawer with the bank; d. That the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must have issued a written statutory demand notice to the drawer, seeking payment of the cheque amount, within 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque unpaid; e. That the drawer of the cheque, despite the receipt of such legal notice, failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the payee or holder in due course within 15 days from the date of such receipt. 32. Only upon proof of the aforementioned ingredients does the offence under Section 138 stand attracted, subject to the operation of statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. These presumptions, however, are rebuttable and impose a reverse burden upon the accused to dislodge the same on a preponderance of probabilities. 33. It is also pertinent to note that, as per the Explanation appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the expression "debt or other liability" refers exclusively to a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This legal clarification is of critical significance, as it makes clear that mere issuance of a cheque is not sufficient to attract penal liability under the statute. The dishonoured cheque must have been issued in discharge of a debt or liability which is subsisting and legally enforceable at the time of its issuance. A cheque issued as a gift, donation, or Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.11/19 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:41 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid towards a time-barred or non-existent liability will not fall within the purview of Section 138 . Thus, the complainant must establish that at the time the cheque was drawn, there existed a valid and enforceable obligation in law for which the cheque was issued. 34. It is well-settled in law that the aforementioned ingredients must co-exist and be satisfied cumulatively in order to constitute the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The absence or non-fulfilment of even one of these statutory requirements is fatal to the prosecution's case and would disentitle the complainant from invoking penal liability against the drawer of the cheque. 35. After hearing the rival contentions from both the parties and perusal of judicial record, it is revealed that the main question in the present case revolves around as to whether there is a material alteration in the impugned cheque? It is apposite at this juncture to reproduce Section 87 NI Act which reads: "87. Effect of material alteration.--Any material alteration of a negotiable instrument renders the same void as against any one who is a party thereto at the time of making such alteration and does not consent thereto, unless it was made in order to carry out the common intention of the original parties. Alteration by indorsee.--And any such alteration, if made by an indorsee, discharges his indorser from all liability to him in respect of the consideration therefor. The provisions of this section are subject to those of sections 20 , 49 , 86 and 125 " 36. It is clear from the plain reading of above section that if a negotiable instrument is materially altered without the consent of the other party then the instrument is void. The law becomes amply clear by the observations made in Jawahar Trading Corporation Vs. K.K. Ramdas 1989 STPL(DC) 10 KER in which it was held that "9. Any material alteration of a negotiable instrument renders the same void against any one who is party thereto at the time of making the Digitally signed by Page no.12/19 SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:43 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid alteration and does not consent thereto, unless it was made in order to carry out the common intention of the original parties. Addition of parties to a contract is a material alteration. Adding stamps and signatures and correction in signatures and writings are also material alterations. Rangayya Naidu v. Sundarammurthy , AIR 1943 Madras 511, relied on by the trial court, is sufficient authority for the position that failing of parties to raise specific pleas in that respect should not deter the court in considering how the law should be applied to proved facts. The principle of law in this respect embodied in Section 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is essential to the integrity and sanctity of contracts. It is intended to prevent fraud and deter men from tampering with written securities. It is repugnant to the policy of law to permit the holder of a negotiable instrument to attempt a fraud of this kind with impunity. By the alteration, the identity of the document itself is destroyed. To hold one liable under the circumstances is to make him liable for a contract which he never agreed. The burden is on the plaintiff in such circumstances to show that the alteration was not improperly made. An alteration which varies the rights, liabilities or legal position of the parties ascertained by the deed in its original state or otherwise varies the legal effect of the instrument as originally expressed, or reduces to certainty some provision which was originally unascertained is a material alteration. To make an alteration material it is not necessary that it should adversely affect the party who raises that plea. In this case, Exts. A1 to A4 executed by first defendant alone not intending to be used as promissory notes were converted into pronotes jointly executed by defendants 1 to 4 with material alterations to that effect. They are definitely hit by Section 87 . The effect of Section 87 is that such a document is void and as such non est. The technical Page no.13/19 SHRUTI Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:45 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid defence of absence of plea should not deter the court in such a situation especially in view of the contention and evidence." 37. The Jawahar Trading case (supra) was relied upon in M/S. Starline Agencies Vs. M/S. R.B. Agencies 2006 STPL(DC) 577 KER where the following observations were made: "4. ............. I find that in the instant case, a detailed discussion as to the issue as to whether the amounts as contended by the appellant and disputed by the accused is due, is not warranted as Ext.P1 cheque so far as the year noted therein is concerned i.e. '96' has been subjected to very manifest material alteration. There is overwriting and the same is done in a crude manner. This court as well as the top court of land has held in unequivocal terms that if an alteration by erasure, interlineation or otherwise, is made in a material part of a deed, after its execution, by or with the consent of any party to or person entitled under it, but without the consent of the party or parties liable under it, the deed is rendered void from the time of the alteration so as to prevent the person who has made or authorised the alteration and those claiming under him, from putting the deed in suit to enforce against any party bound by it who did not consent to the alteration, any obligation, covenant or promise thereby undertaken or made...." 38. Further, in Kedar Jagannath Acharya Vs. Mohsin Yasin Momin 2008 STPL(DC) 850 BOM it was observed: '3. After the trial, the learned trial Court acquitted the respondent observing that not only in several bills about supply of goods but in the cheque also there was overwriting and alteration. It was noted that cheque was actually dated 18th December, 1998 and therefore, it could be presented to the bank for encashment on or before 18-6- Digitally signed Page no.14/19 SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:49 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid 1999. Cheque was presented on 27-6-1999 that is beyond the period of six months being the period of validity of the cheque. To bring the cheque within limitation the date "18-12-1998" on the cheque was altered as "3-1-1999". Alteration was neither initialled by the respondent nor there was any evidence that alteration or change in the date was made with consent of the respondent. As per the banking rules, nobody is expected to make alteration in the cheque and if it becomes necessary, alteration must be duly signed by the drawer of the cheque. In view of this, the learned trial Court found that when the cheque was presented on 27-6-1999 it was beyond it's validity period and besides the other ground, on this ground itself the accused/respondent was entitled to be acquitted.'" 39. Further in Amarjit Singh Vs. Nazar Singh 2010 STPL(DC) 692 P&H , it was observed: '9. Adverting to the facts of the instant case, the plaintiff who is seeking the enforcement of the promissory note has not explained as to when and how the stated alteration was made. In absence of such explanation, he must fail as onus is upon him to show that the material alteration was made either with consent of parties or in order to effectuate common intention of parties. In absence of such plea, presumption is that the material alteration was made subsequently. Sequelly, the disputed pronote is void under Section 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The second substantial question of law is determined accordingly. In consequence of the preceding discussion, this appeal fails and is dismissed.'" 40. Thus the law is well crystallised that material alteration unless made with the consent of the parties and unless made in order to carry out the common intention Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.15/19 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:51 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid of parties, renders the instrument void. The burden lies on the person who alleges that the alteration is done with the consent of the other party. In the present case, there is a crude alteration in the date mentioned on the cheque which is not appended with the signatures of the accused. It is clear that the alteration in date amounts to material alteration. Reliance is placed upon Bpd Investments (Pvt.) Ltd Vs. Maple Leaf Trading International (Pvt.) Ltd. 2006 STPL(DC) 719 DEL where it was held that: '9. Upon a reading of the aforesaid section, it becomes clear that if there is a material alterations of the kind referred to in a cheque then the cheque would become void. What is to be noted however are the two considerations indicated in the section itself. For a cheque or other negotiable instrument to remain valid despite material alterations, the material alteration must be with the consent of the other party and unless it was made towards the furtherance of a common intention. In other words if the alteration is consented to by the parties then, even if it is material, it will not render the instrument void. Moreover, if the alteration is made towards the common intention of the parties then again such an alteration would not render the instrument void. In the context of the facts of the present case, the learned Counsel for the applicant/defendant submitted that the I two undated cheques were obviously dated subsequently by the plaintiff on or before the time of presentation of the said cheques which is alleged to have been done on 2.7.2003. Therefore, it amounts to the situation where the date of an instrument is altered. That an alteration in a date on a negotiable instrument amounts to a material alteration in the terms indicated under Section 87 , has been made clear by various decisions referred to Digitally by the learned Counsel being : signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 Page no.16/19 16:46:53 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid 1. K.M. Basappa & Another v. Patel Marule Gowda & Another , AIR (38) 1951 Mysore 2. Vakkalagadda Kondiah v. Channamsetty Pedda Pulliah and Others , AIR 1960 AP 121. 3. Atlampati Subba Reddy v. Neelapareddi , AIR 1966 AP 267. 4. Jayantilal Goel v. Smt. Zubeda Khanum , AIR 1986 AP 120' 41. In the present case, the central issue for adjudication concerns the alteration of the date appearing on the impugned cheque and its legal effect under the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 . The determination of this issue requires careful consideration of whether such alteration was made with the consent, knowledge, or authority of the Accused, or whether it was effected unilaterally by the Complainant to suit his convenience. 42. It is a settled proposition of law that where any material alteration is made in a negotiable instrument without the consent of all parties liable thereon, the instrument becomes void as against those parties who did not consent to the change. Section 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act explicitly declares that any material alteration made without such consent renders the instrument void, except in certain limited circumstances expressly permitted by law. The underlying rationale is that a negotiable instrument, being a document of value that carries rights and liabilities, must reflect the mutual intention of its parties at the time of execution. Any alteration which alters the legal relationship of the parties or the time, mode, or conditions of payment strikes at the root of the instrument's authenticity and thereby vitiates it. In the present factual matrix, the alleged alteration pertains to the date of issuance of the cheque. If the alteration of this date had been effected with the consent of the Accused, the instrument would have continued to remain valid in law, as such consent would demonstrate mutual intention to extend or adjust the period of presentment. However, if the alteration was made unilaterally by the Digitally signed Page no.17/19 by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:55 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid Complainant , without the knowledge or approval of the Accused, it would constitute a "material alteration" within the meaning of Section 87 and would render the cheque void ab initio. The decisions in Jawahar Trading v. Ramesh Chand and Amarjit Singh v. State of Punjab have firmly laid down that the burden of proving that a disputed alteration was made with the consent and authorization of the drawer lies squarely on the Complainant. This burden arises because the Complainant seeks to derive a legal advantage based on the altered instrument and thus must establish the legitimacy of the alteration. In the case at hand, the Accused has categorically denied having made, authorized, or consented to any alteration in the date of the cheque. The alteration is apparent and palpable upon a mere visual inspection of the instrument. Significantly, the cheque has remained throughout in the possession and control of the Complainant, which further imposes upon him a heightened duty to explain the circumstances under which the alteration occurred. 43. Despite this, the Complainant has failed to produce any credible evidence, either oral or documentary, to show that the alteration was carried out with the knowledge, direction, or consent of the Accused. No contemporaneous correspondence, acknowledgment, or surrounding circumstance has been brought on record to establish a common understanding or intention between the parties regarding the change in date. The Complainant has also not offered any satisfactory explanation as to when, how, or by whom the alteration was made. Such absence of explanation renders the Complainant's version doubtful and incapable of supporting the presumption of regularity in execution. In light of these facts and the settled legal position, this Court finds that the Complainant has failed to discharge the burden that law casts upon him. The alteration in the date of the impugned cheque is material, visible, and demonstrably made without the consent of the drawer. The said alteration, therefore, squarely attracts the provisions of Section 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which operate to render the instrument void to Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.18/19 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.10 16:46:57 +0530 Ct case no. 6186/2018 Abdur Rasheed Vs. Shahid the extent of the alteration. 44. Consequently, the cheque in question cannot be treated as a valid and enforceable instrument for the purposes of invoking penal liability under Section 138 of the Act. Accordingly, it is held that the impugned cheque stands vitiated by a material alteration made without the consent of the Accused and to his manifest prejudice. The present complaint, therefore, does not meet the essential legal requirements of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and the Accused is entitled to the benefit thereof. Conclusion 44. In the light of the aforementioned discussion, the complainant has successfully proved all the ingredients of Section 138 NI Act. Accordingly, this court holds accused Mr. Shahid not guilty for committing the offence under section 138 of the NI Act and he is hereby acquitted. 45.
